## Building resilient surgical systems that can withstand external shocks

ABSTRACT When surgical systems fail, there is the major collateral impact on patients, society and economies. While short-­ term impact on patient outcomes during periods of high system stress is easy to measure, the long-­term repercussions of global crises are harder to quantify and require modelling studies with inherent uncertainty. When external stressors such as high-­threat infectious disease, forced migration or climate-­change-­related events occur, there is a resulting surge in healthcare demand. This, directly and indirectly, affects perioperative pathways, increasing pressure on emergency, critical and operative care areas. While different stressors have different effects on healthcare systems, they share the common feature of exposing the weakest areas, at which point care pathways breakdown. Surgery has been identified as a highly vulnerable area for early failure. Despite efforts by the WHO to improve preparedness in the wake of the SARS-­CoV-­2 pandemic, measurement of healthcare investment and surgical preparedness metrics suggests that surgical care is not yet being prioritised by policy-­makers. Investment in the ‘response’ phase of health system recovery without investment in the ‘readiness’ phase will not mitigate long-­ term health effects for patients as new stressors arise. This analysis aims to explore how surgical preparedness can be measured, identify emerging threats and explore their potential impact on surgical services. Finally, it aims to highlight the role of high-­quality research in developing resilient surgical systems.

INTRODUCTION A health system is the collection of people, institutions and resources that aim to improve, protect, maintain and restore health.1 Surgical services are an ‘indivisible and indispensable’ component of these systems. Surgical system resilience draws on engineering concepts and describes the ability of an interconnected perioperative system to adapt its functioning to absorb a significant external event (a ‘shock’) and transform, if necessary, to recover from this event. This may bring a system back to its original equilibrium or into a new equilibrium (a ‘transformative shock’).2

Weaknesses in surgical pathways can undermine healthcare provision in both secondary and community care.3 4 Such weaknesses can develop when systems are functioning under normal conditions (often due to chronic underfunding) but are exposed and intensified by external shocks.5–7 The SaRS-­CoV-­2 pandemic has illustrated this at a global scale, leading to redeployment of the surgical workforce, millions of delayed operations and significant harm for patients from increased severity of disease presentation.8 9 However, other external shocks have shaped surgical and health systems in a variety of contexts in recent years (eg, Ebola in West Africa,10 Conflict in Ukraine,11 Sudden-­onset disasters in Haiti12) and are expected to occur with increasing frequency and intensity in coming

SUMMARY BOX

⇒Surgical systems are a core pillar of comprehensive healthcare systems. Investing in building resilience to surgical pathways and networks strengthens population-­level health and economic productivity. ⇒Assessing the readiness of surgical systems for external shocks is complex. Tools such as the WHO Situational Assessment Tool and Surgical Preparedness Index (SPI) can support transdisciplinary evaluation of interconnected services, pathways and providers but new approaches are needed. ⇒Timing of external system shocks can be unpredictable. Strategic investment in preparedness based on a local context can strengthen components of perioperative systems at greatest threat. ⇒Governments and policy-­makers must invest in surgical system preparedness to ensure their populations’ health, social and economic well-­being. Sequential measures of SPI suggest that readiness is not currently being prioritised, which risks serious collateral societal impact. ⇒Collaborative research efforts to evaluate and implement methods to strengthen surgical systems are required to inform government and supranational initiatives.

To do so means moving from a place of crisis response and recovery to system readiness and resilience.14 15

Surgical system deficits are exposed by external ‘shocks’ for three principal reasons. First, unexpected external events can create a surge in demand for surgical services including for infection, maternity and trauma, thus directly increasing pressure on the surgical system itself.16 Second, the surgical ecosystem is often called to action in healthcare crises. For example, during the SARS-­CoV-­2 pandemic, the perioperative workforce, supply chain and infrastructure were all critical to the global response, further highlighting the codependency of surgical systems with broader human health.17 Third, surgical services are often deprioritised for funding by policy-­makers at the expense of areas seen to be more politically important (eg, infectious disease, primary care).18

Surgical services intersect with almost every aspect of the broader healthcare system, from primary care to complex tertiary care, community-­based rehabilitation and follow-­up. Initiatives such as the WHO’s Emergency Medical Teams are critical in disaster response; however, they are not designed to provide comprehensive support to a surgical system, including non-­urgent essential care. Surgical system preparedness, therefore, involves assessing multidimensional surgical systems, including facility readiness, workforce, quality, coverage, safety, systemwide integration and actioning findings to build resilience.

AIM This analysis has three central aims: (1) to explore how surgical system resilience can be measured and to review global progress; (2) to highlight high-­priority threats to health systems and explore how these might impact surgical services and (3) to identify collaborative research opportunities to progress the surgical preparedness and resilience agenda.

ASSESSING SURGICAL SYSTEM PREPAREDNESS Assessing surgical system resilience is complex and requires numerous methods, tools and metrics. Resilience can be evaluated at multiple levels, including locally (hospital), regionally or nationally (across an entire system). The WHO Service Availability and Readiness Assessment (WHO SARA) provides a framework to quantify surgical facility resources and capacity across the domains of infrastructure and consumables, service delivery, workforce, financing and information management.19 However, there are also qualitative aspects to system assessment. The Safe Surgery Organizational Readiness Tool, a theory-­based and evidence-­based

instrument, looks through a different lens, assessing the qualitative readiness of facility leaders and caregivers for implementing safety and quality interventions.20 The Surgical Preparedness Index (SPI) uses 23 globally applicable indicators of system preparedness that can be assessed by front-­line staff and policy-­makers. The SPI was shown to be relevant at a national and subnational level and is an important method for hospitals to conduct annual self-­assessments.21 These are three lenses through which to view surgical system strength and preparedness; however, each is limited in scope. For example, data from the COVID-­19 pandemic suggests that surgical services that would be considered ‘strong’ (eg, highest resource settings) in a WHO SARA evaluation, may have a low ability to recover from an external shock. A hospital’s SPI was strongly associated with its ability to maintain activity during a period of external stress but is unable to evaluation overall capacity, workforce or infrastructure strength. Therefore, it is critical to (1) assess surgical systems from multiple dimensions using these tools and (2) consider and how they support resilience within wider healthcare systems.

Changes in surgical system preparedness and investment over time Changes in surgical system preparedness have been measured over time in three sequential annual studies since 202121–231: SPI measurement (June–August 2021),2 CovidSurg-­3 cohort study (February 2022),3 HernIas, Pathway and Planetary Outcomes for Inguinal Hernia Surgery (HIPPO) cohort study (January–March 2023). Where multiple assessments were made of the same hospital, the mean was calculated first by indicator, then an overall mean index score for the hospital was calculated as an aggregate mean of these means. Only hospitals with at least one SPI measurement across all three assessment periods were included. Results were summarised for each year both overall and for each indicator, and as the mean of all hospitals’ mean SPI scores and presented with a 95% CI. These data demonstrate that despite a significant impetus to strengthen surgical systems in the wake of the COVID-­19 pandemic, there have been only marginal temporal gains globally across the SPI indicators (figure 1). While countries have sought to address the global waiting list crisis in different ways to prevent further harm to patients from delays and cancellation of surgery, there is still significant room for improvement in system preparedness.24

To explore the relationship between national mean SPI scores and relevant global health indicators, generalised additive models were fitted using penalised cubic splines with shrinkage. Only countries with five or more hospital-­level assessments across all three studies were included. The four selected indicators were (1) UN Human Development Index, which is a composite index of life expectancy, education and per capita income (a higher Human Development Index score indicates greater development); (2) global health security index,

Analyses were done with R Studio (V.4.1.1) packages: tidyverse, finalfit, psych and ggplot2. The dichotomy between emergency and elective surgical systems is a structural division, not necessarily based on disease biology. For example, for a patient with a symptomatic inguinal (groin) hernia the difference between an emergency and elective operation is driven by health beliefs, financial coverage and timing of presentation to a hospital with surgical services.26 Properly functioning surgical systems require a dynamic link between emergency and elective systems at every level. Elective systems must have short waiting lists and sufficient surplus resources to withstand external disturbances and still function. At the same time, emergency systems should be able to quickly flex and expand (usually using elective services) as needed during increased demand due to external stressors.21 24 The interdependence between elective and emergency systems emphasises the need to avoid strengthening one at the expense of the other. Instead, a balanced planning approach is essential, recognising that both are integral to a comprehensive surgical system. When elective surgery systems fail, this drives demand for emergency surgical care, leading to higher-­risk procedures associated with additional adverse outcomes. This puts additional burden on the whole system, exacerbating a feedback response loop

in response to external stressors that can lead to health systems’ collapse. Investment in the ‘response’ phase of health system recovery without investment in the ‘readiness’ phase, also fails to address the long-­term health needs of populations as new system stressors arise.27 This is reflected by chronic global underfunding of system preparedness as shown in data from the Organisation for Economic Co-­operation and Development. Despite unprecedented global investment in pandemic preparedness during COVID-­ 19, only 17 of 137 low-­income and middle-­income countries (LMICs) will be able to increase health spending in line with the G20’s high-­level panel recommendations between 2022 and 2026, putting these populations at even greater risk.28 Surgery is the most vulnerable service during system crises and despite formal declaration of surgical care as a global priority at the World Health Assembly in 2015 and 2023 and significant advocacy efforts of NIHR Global Surgery, the G4 Alliance, World Federation of Societies of Anaesthesiologists and others, remains critically underfunded and underprepared.4 29 30

EMERGING EXTERNAL STRESSORS The nature of external shocks on healthcare systems is that their timing is often unpredictable and collateral impacts can be hard to measure. Direct impacts on patient outcomes and healthcare costs are often immediately measurable. However, the long-­term physical, psychological and economic impact requires modelling studies with inherent uncertainty. Investing in surgical system strengthening is also about investing in wider healthcare services that can cope with the direct and indirect pressures of external system shocks and sustain accessible, timely, high-­quality care for elective and emergency presentations of disease. This will minimise the impact of these shocks on the short-­term and long-­term health of populations. The World Economic Forum has defined 36 current ‘global risks’ and their interconnection in their 2024 Global Risks report.31 In this section, we reflect on six evolving external stressors that are likely to impact surgical systems over the next 5 years. Impact of external shocks on surgical systems resilience Different stressors are likely to have varying impacts on components of perioperative care delivery. The nature of surgical systems is that if one component fails this may lead to failure of entire surgical pathways and/or surgical safety, owing to the interdependence of system components. To support individualised efforts to improve local system preparedness based on the likelihood of external stressors, we predicted the impact of six highlighted external stressors on each preparedness indicator (figure 3). The potential impact on each indicator was estimated as high (red), moderate (orange) or low (green) by a diverse range of members from the expert writing group (N=5), with moderate agreement (ICC 0.64 (95% CI 0.55 to 0.73)). In a discussion forum, final

consensus was reached. The raters consider the system stressors to have a very variable impact on the 23 indicators, explored in greater detail in the following section. Consistently ‘Systems’ indicators, such as predischarge and postdischarge care, social support and interhospital transfer, and ‘Staffing’ indicators such as staff redistribution and ring-­fenced teams were at highest risk of failure. Further evidence is needed to measure these impacts in real-­world data.

High-threat infectious diseases SPIs at highest risk: Facilities and consumables, staffing, systems

as 18.2 million individuals, and the longer-­term impact of reduced access to care for both non-­COVID acute conditions and chronic conditions will continue for generations to come.33 34 In the context of surgery, COVID-­19 both increased perioperative risks of infection and death and sparked a global waiting list crisis, with millions of operations delayed or cancelled.9 35 36 Moreover, the United Nations estimates that the pandemic cost the global economy over US$8.5 trillion between 2020 and 2022 and plunged an additional 34 million people below the poverty line.37 This has negatively impacted economic capacity and political priority for making the investments required to strengthen surgical systems against existing weaknesses and future shocks. Even before the COVID-­19 pandemic, viral outbreaks were known to have devastating impacts on surgical systems. During the Ebola outbreak of 2013–2016 in West Africa (box  1), surgical services were significantly reduced across Liberia, Sierra Leone and Guinea.38 In some cases, surgical services and/or hospitals in affected regions were closed due to shortages in healthcare workers, unavailability of protective equipment, fears of transmission and inadequate training and supplies to support a well-­functioning surgical system while also protecting patients and healthcare workers from exposure to the virus39; high rates of mortality were documented among healthcare workers due to occupational exposure to the virus. By some estimates, the indirect impact of the Ebola epidemic on population health and mortality far exceeded the direct impact of the virus on itself.40 41 The WHO defines Disease ‘X’ as a new, unexpected emergence of a transmissible disease that humans have not yet been exposed to and demonstrates high transmissibility and severity of disease.42 While we cannot, by definition, anticipate when the next ‘Disease X’ will emerge, policy-­makers must increase investment in health security relevant to surgical system resilience and preparedness. This will ensure continuity of access to surgery and delivery of surgical services in the face of different infectious disease threats.

Forced migration SPIs at highest risk: Systems

Analysis As highlighted by a 2018 Lancet Commission, health and migration are closely linked.43 They are interwoven in a dynamic process that can profoundly impact the health of individuals and vulnerable communities throughout the migration cycle, including origin, transit, destination and return—particularly in cases of forced migration. As populations affected by conflict, sudden-­onset disasters and climate change rise, so do the number of people displaced. This has reached an all-­time high in 2023 at 110 million displaced individuals and refugees.44 Despite political rhetoric, this commonly occurs within (internally displaced) and between (refugees) LMICs rather than affecting high-­income health systems; LMIC health systems are often at critical capacity due to internal

Political instability and surgical system preparedness in Mexico LM, National Insitute of Health Research (NIHR) Global Health Research Unit on Global Surgery, Veracruz, Mexico 15 years after its inception, the System of Social Protection for Health (Sistema de Protección Social en Salud) and Popular Insurance (Seguro Popular) were dismantled in 2019 due to political pressure to solve the ‘corruption’ that supposedly plagued it.72 Seguro Popular was a restructure of the Mexican Health System aimed to break the poverty and employment status barriers and to finally achieve universal health coverage. This programme provided protection to around 75% of the population who previously had no health insurance coverage (>50 million people) and significantly reduced out-­of-­pocket and catastrophic expenditure among the Mexican population.73 In January 2020, just before the emergence of COVID-­19, Mexico transitioned from Seguro Popular, a programme in which states oversaw health, to Instituto de Salud para el Bienestar (INSABI), a new centralised system.74 This new project had no piloting and few operational rules and came into effect at the same time as the pandemic. These factors are felt to have contributed to Mexico being one of the countries with the highest excess mortality during the pandemic. During the last year of the current government, INSABI has yet again been replaced by a new system. Whether Seguro Popular was the solution to having a system able to provide universal access, equity and quality healthcare, will remain unknown. Moreover, what is clear is that healthcare systems should be protected from political polarisation, volatility and impulsiveness and instead direct efforts towards reforming programs depending on objective evaluation of their results and evidence-­based health needs of populations.

The impact of multiple system stressors on surgery in Haiti KC, Former Medecins sans Frontieres (MSF) Board and Director for the Centre for Global Surgery at Stellenbosch University, South Africa. Haiti is the poorest country in the Americas and is plagued by political instability, sudden-­onset disaster and increasing violence. At baseline, the health system was fragile and with little access to surgical care for those in rural communities, and little preparedness in the event of severe system stress. In 2008, a series of hurricanes in the Arbonite region resulted in severe flooding that destroyed thousands of homes and health facilities including the hospital in the town of Gonaives. The humanitarian medical organisation, MSF established emergency surgical services by constructing a temporary hospital in a warehouse. Within several weeks, a working pharmacy, inpatient wards, an emergency room and operating theatre were constructed. In 12 weeks, 330 procedures were performed with a low complication rate. Emergency obstetrical, trauma and non-­trauma operations were performed with caesarean section for obstructed labour as the most common procedure. Poor sanitation resulted in a high incidence of typhoid infection and ileal typhoid perforation was a common abdominal emergency in children. At the time, there was only fully trained anaesthesiologist in Haiti. However, in previous years, MSF had trained several nurse anaesthetists who provided anaesthesia along with an expatriate team.75 After 3 months, the flood waters receded, and the MSF team withdrew. Humanitarian organisations can provide temporary surgical services when an external threat (hurricane) decimates the existing health system. However, when that existing health system was unable address most surgical conditions at baseline, the decision of when to withdraw is difficult.55 Non-­governmental organisations provide up to 40% of

Fiscal and economic shocks SPIs at highest risk: Facilities and consumables, systems

Analysis Economics and health are intimately linked. Economic crises can affect health across the life course, from altering health determinants and risk behaviours to impacting the affordability and resourcing of services and systems.47 There has been a severe global financial contraction as well as inflation as a result of COVID-­19 pandemic, which continues to have spillover effects on inequality, productivity and health despite a multilateral policy response.48 For example, in Venezuela, the ‘double-­hit’ of hyperinflation and pandemic recovery has led to a 40% increase in infant deaths and a 3.5-­year decrease in adult life expectancy, largely due to collapse of maternity and trauma services.49 While surgery can be perceived by policy-­makers as an expensive luxury, it forms a fundamental component of basic health systems. Surgery forms part of the treatment pathway for up to 40% of all non-­communicable disease, including trauma and cancer50 and infections such as osteomyelitis and cholecystitis. Providing surgery is very cost-­effective for governments, and the failure to support surgical care has profound impacts on countries economic and societal productivity.51 As surgical pathways are integrated across many components of primary and secondary care, they are uniquely vulnerable to recessions and disruptions in capital flow. Protecting access to surgical care during economic hardship is a fundamental component of an equitable, comprehensive healthcare system.

Environmental risks & sudden-onset disasters SPIs at highest risk: Facilities and consumables, staffing, prioritisation, systems

Analysis Climate change is becoming one of the major drivers of weather-­related sudden-­onset disasters.52 The number of climate-­related disasters has tripled in the last 30 years and the cost of climate adaptation to developing countries is estimated at around US$140–US$300 billion per year by 2030.13 53 Disasters can destroy or damage surgical

Impact of Ebola virus disease on surgical care in West Africa 2014–2016 JM, Co-­Director of the WHO Collaborating Centre for Global Surgery, Anesthesia & Perioperative care, Western University, Canada Ebola virus disease (EVD) outbreaks have occurred sporadically in countries of Africa since the first recorded outbreak in 1974. Transmission of Ebola virus occurs via contact with contaminated fluid, body tissues or through infectious airborne droplets. The largest EVD outbreak to date remains the epidemic of West Africa in 2014–2016, resulting in more than 28 600 reported cases and 11 325 deaths primarily across Guinea, Sierra Leone and Liberia. Like other viral epidemics (including SARS in 2003), healthcare workers were disproportionately affected. More than 513 healthcare workers deaths were reported in West Africa, representing an estimated loss of 1%, 7% and 8% of the healthcare workforce due to EVD in Guinea, Sierra Leone and Liberia, respectively (US Centers for Disease Control 2019). Several surgeons, anaesthesia providers and perioperative team members were infected or died.76 Since countries of West Africa have <0.7/100 000 surgeons, obstetricians and anaesthesia providers (about 10-­fold lower than high-­income countries), these losses were a staggering example of the direct impact of an epidemic on ability to provide surgical care, in a country that already had a vulnerable population due to very few surgeons prior to the epidemic.30 During the epidemic, deficiencies of the already-­vulnerable healthcare system were laid bare. Many healthcare workers who were attempting to provide continued routine care experienced lack of infrastructure and resources to deliver care safely during the epidemic, including lack of access to personal protective equipment in the surgical setting (many described having to buy their own protective equipment, and even then, not having access to high-­grade biosafety masks, visors, drapes). There was also a lack of protocols and equipment for infection prevention and control in the surgical setting where exposure to infectious bodily fluids is a high risk, lack of access to diagnostic tools to adequately test for EVD in patients with conditions that had symptom overlap with EVD and lack of access to decontamination protocols for surgical equipment during the pandemic.40 During the Ebola epidemic, surgical volumes dropped by more than 41% in Sierra Leone in the first year, and some hospitals closed due to a lack of healthcare workers and a fear of potential exposure to EVD by both patients and healthcare workers.77 By most estimates, the indirect impact of the Ebola outbreak was orders of magnitude greater than the direct impact of the virus on deaths and loss of health-­related quality of life, due to the reduced capacity to the sudden decrease in access to hospital care, reduced access to surgical care and reduced access to primary care services for other conditions unrelated to Ebola.78 After the EVD epidemic of 2014–2016, there was increased global recognition of the vulnerability of healthcare systems, especially surgical systems, to high-­risk infectious disease outbreaks. However, a global approach to readiness and response to infectious disease outbreaks for the surgical setting remains to be delineated. In addition, there has been little sustained investment in protecting surgical settings from vulnerabilities to epidemic threats to access to care and preventing transmission risks for surgical teams and patients.79

As well as the increased demand for surgical services from traumatically injured patients, surgical personnel can also be injured, evacuated or otherwise unable to work, reducing surgical capacity.54 While there are NGOs that specialise in disaster responses, they must be coordinated and invited by national or provincial governments, else risk greater harm than good (eg, Earthquakes in Nepal).55 Stocking surgical supplies in hospitals in case of a disaster is difficult when many low-­resourced settings barely have supplies to do their planned cases, and the very nature of sudden-­onset disasters is unpredictable. However, having a ‘disaster preparedness plan’ with the surgical team can be helpful, both in terms of triaging patients and the wider system response of outreach, collaboration, leadership and establishing a responsive workforce and supply chains; this may also include international collaboration. Information systems casemix and outcome data during disasters can be extremely helpful for future planning, justifying ongoing investment in system preparedness and measuring quality of care. If standardised databases are set up predisaster and used,

this makes routine data collection during a disaster more streamlined and acceptable.

Political instability and conflict SPIs at highest risk: Facilities and consumables, staffing, prioritisation, systems

Analysis Political instability, changes in governance, fluctuating political prioritisation and shifting power structures can directly impact the capacity and capability to deliver surgical care. Financing structures and service commissioning can be disrupted, increasing system inequalities and the risk of moral injury to healthcare providers (box 1). Where political instability leads to conflict, this can rapidly destroy infrastructure, increase attacks on healthcare workers, disrupt critical supply chains and drive demand for emergency surgical care, limiting the ability to deliver planned surgery. Long-­term planning and investment are required to strengthen surgical systems—particularly in health workforce development. This is often in direct tension with the shorter-­term returns on investment that governments and political parties are looking to achieve within a given electoral cycle.56 In countries where healthcare delivery

Unfortunately, the health implications of political instability are often most pronounced for the most vulnerable populations in society including children, those living with disability and those economically or structurally marginalised.57 In some conflict and postconflict settings, military–civilian cooperation has successfully increased the resilience of surgical systems, in addition to more established partnerships with NGOs.

Loss of surgical workforce SPIs at highest risk: Staffing, systems

Analysis Another important but often overlooked factor that threatens surgical systems, particularly in LMICs, is the sustained, unfettered and unrelenting loss of the surgical workforce away from areas of high unmet surgical need.58 This can be experienced as internal migration, from rural and district settings to urban settings, from the public to the private sector, and as emigration, typically to higher-­ income countries. Some of the reasons for emigration by surgeons included lack of professional fulfilment due to poor infrastructure, little or no research funding, limited career structure and advancement, insecurity and increasing spates of violence, and lack of educational opportunities for their children. Recent evidence suggests that Africa’s surgeon, anaesthetist and obstetrician density is about 0.7/100 000 population, which is a far cry from the Lancet Commission’s recommended average of 20/100 000.59 60 Sadly, the situation worsens, and some hospitals are shutting down wards and theatres due to lack of healthcare workers to staff them. Workforce challenges can also be experienced in high-­income countries, particularly those with large geographic areas (eg, Australia), low population density (eg, Norway) or challenging climatic conditions (eg, Canada). These regions also chronically suffer from surgical workforce loss or inadequate surgical service coverage. Measures to improve the surgical workforce include increasing training slots of institutions by the regulatory authorities and adapting and adopting technology to make high-­quality educational resources available through webinars and online training platforms, and exchange programmes for exposure to surgical competencies.61 Perhaps the most important of these solutions is the political will and commensurate investment to improve conditions of service and provide adequate infrastructure and resources to strengthen existing health systems.

RESEARCH OPPORTUNITIES IN SURGICAL PREPAREDNESS Fortifying surgical services and systems against external pressures requires an essential triad of high-­quality data analytics, pragmatic research and the implementation of learning health systems. As was seen in the COVID-­19 pandemic, the presence of these elements differentiates

health systems that can successfully reconfigure in the face of external threats.62

Real-­time healthcare data can serve as a backbone, providing an empirical foundation for understanding systemic weaknesses and identifying actionable solutions. This should extend beyond traditional methods to encompass cutting-­edge technologies like artificial intelligence.63 When applied thoughtfully, these technologies can enhance surgical decision-­making (eg, personalised risk stratification) and adaptability (eg, intelligent workforce and resource planning), especially in high-­pressure environments.64 Important conclusions, however, can be drawn from simple but high-­quality data. For instance, the COVIDSurg-­GlobalSurg study of 140K patients provided timely evidence to support evidence-­ based globally relevant policy guidance in delivering safe surgery to patients after a SARS-­CoV-­2 diagnosis.65 The HIPPO study used inguinal hernia as tracer condition to evaluate the building blocks of quality, safety, access and coverage to support evidence-­based recommendations for strengthening elective surgery pathways.26 During shocks, real-­time data such as this have the potential to inform the safety and effectiveness of service reconfiguration, for example, which operations to prioritise, how to reallocate teams, protective equipment and protocols, as well as responding to changes patterns of disease. Research, particularly operational research, plays a critical role in developing innovative solutions. Novel approaches to improve resilience are complex interventions: they are multidimensional, target a range of behaviours, often require human interaction and are evaluated using several outcomes.66 Specific approaches to their development, feasibility testing, evaluation and implementation are required. Crucial to this is early and broad stakeholder engagement, ensuring that early concepts are robust and account for contextual and cultural differences across settings. This is being demonstrated currently in the Wellcome Leap SAVE programme in collaboration with the NIHR Global Health Research Unit on Global Surgery, which seeks to improve both access to surgery and postoperative safety in LMICs using novel technologies.67 Research conclusions should be broadly generalisable across health systems. To achieve this, we must be constantly asking, not only if an intervention works, but why it works and in which contexts. This requires deep engagement and involvement of patients and a greater use of applied health methods drawn from implementation science, health services and policy. The concept of learning health systems is central to all these approaches—a model that integrates routine healthcare delivery with continuous learning. In such systems, every patient encounter is an opportunity for data collection, analysis and learning, ensuring that the healthcare system is constantly evolving and adapting, thus increasing its capacity to withstand external pressures.68 This is easy to say and difficult to do in all health systems, but particularly in low-­resource settings. Health system research also has a role to play in reducing the risk of critical stress events, for example, by providing evidence to decarbonise surgical care pathways. One example of this is the GreenSurg programme, which is has deeply engaged multidisciplinary researchers, policy-­makers and industry to drive decarbonisation of health systems through sharing innovations, developing a streamlined data collection platform and robust evaluation of measures to improve sustainability across the surgical system.70

Strengthening surgical systems through research not only enhances immediate preparedness but lays the foundation for future resilience across the broader health system in the face of evolving challenges. The recently integrated Emergency, Critical and Operative Care resolution emphasised the interdependent role these components play in the effective delivery of health system-­wide services, such as the treatment of injury, infection, mental health conditions, acute exacerbations of noncommunicable diseases, acute complications of pregnancy and other health conditions, including in neonates and children.71 By fostering a culture of continuous learning and adaptation, health systems can better withstand and thrive amidst external pressures. A conceptual map of research efforts in surgical preparedness throughout the perioperative journey is displayed in figure 4.

CONCLUSION There has never been a more critical time to address surgical system preparedness and resilience. Surgery is a foundational pillar of health services and systems. Recent global events including the SARS-­CoV-­2 pandemic, economic recession, extreme weather events and regional conflicts have demonstrated how vulnerable surgical systems can be to external shocks, with immediate and long-­term impacts on population health. Identifying factors that protect surgical systems from external shocks, and evaluating the resilience of local, national and global surgical systems is an important first step in advancing the surgical preparedness and resilience agenda. Several collaborative research groups and multilateral agencies are advancing efforts in this area. However, to drive meaningful change and to significantly strengthen health services and systems to the myriad of future stressors and shocks policy-­makers must address the complexity of surgery and, more broadly, hospital-­ based services in how they design, finance and deliver healthcare. This will require not just a change in national and global health politics and mindsets but also a focus on research germane to surgical resilience across a range of threats, from climate change to new pandemics.
